summary: Describes how a device with limited storage and bandwidth can stream audio and video attachments from an IMAP server instead of downloading them fully. It describes a profile of existing mail features for the job. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of downloading a whole movie before you watch, you start watching as it comes. This does that for video and sound attached to email.

questions: play video attachment on mobile mail
subtitle: Stream audio and video email attachments instead of downloading them fully.

tldr.problem: Mobile and resource-constrained devices struggle to download and store large video or audio attachments from email, due to bandwidth limits and storage constraints.
tldr.mechanism: A media server retrieves a message attachment from an IMAP server using an authorized URL and streams it to the device using RTP, allowing playback to begin immediately.
tldr.outcome: Users can play media attachments without downloading the entire file, though the media cannot be accessed offline.

today: RFC 5616 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a profile for streaming email attachments that combines multiple existing standards and remains available for implementation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Email clients on devices with limited storage and bandwidth, such as mobile phones, face a challenge: large video and audio attachments take a long time to download and may not fit in the device's storage. For media such as voice mail, video clips, and audio attachments, streaming offers a solution. Instead of downloading the entire attachment, the device can stream it using the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), allowing playback to start quickly.

This RFC describes a profile that combines existing technologies: IMAP's URLAUTH extension for secure access to message parts, the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) with media server profiles, and RTP for streaming. The approach assumes a media server acts as an intermediary, fetching media from the IMAP server and streaming it to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine asking a librarian to read a book aloud to you instead of printing it. The librarian is the media server, the book is in your email (IMAP server), and they stream the words to you.

sections.title: The Three-Party Architecture
sections.content:
The mechanism involves three main components: the email client, the IMAP server, and the media server. The client discovers a message part (such as a video) and generates a special authorized IMAP URL using the GENURLAUTH command. This URL grants the media server permission to retrieve the message part without the client being able to access it directly.

The client then contacts the media server via SIP, passing the authorized URL. The media server uses this URL to fetch the attachment from the IMAP server, then streams the media to the client using RTP. The media server acts as a trusted intermediary, allowing the message part to be accessed by a device that may lack storage for the entire file.
sections.plainLanguage: Three players: your phone (client), your email service (IMAP), and a helper service (media server). Your phone asks the email service for a ticket to retrieve a video, gives the ticket to the helper, and the helper gets the video and streams it back to your phone.

sections.title: Two Streaming Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC describes two methods for setting up streaming, with different levels of control. The announcement service (RFC 4240) is simpler: the client sends a SIP INVITE to a special 'annc' user at the media server, supplying the authorized URL in the request. The media server retrieves the media and begins streaming immediately, with no further control from the client.

The MSCML IVR service (RFC 5022) is more complex but offers VCR-style controls such as pause, fast-forward, and rewind. The client establishes a SIP session with the media server, then sends an XML request with media control instructions. The media server allows the client to control playback using DTMF tones (phone keypad digits) or explicit commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Simple mode: ask the helper to play a video, and they stream it. Advanced mode: ask the helper to play, and then you can tell them to pause, skip forward, or rewind using your remote control.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The authorized IMAP URL is a security token. The client can request it with an 'anonymous' access identifier, allowing any media server to fetch the message part, or with a 'stream' identifier, which restricts access to media servers that the IMAP server recognizes. The client SHOULD use the 'stream' access identifier when the media server has a pre-existing trust relationship with the IMAP server.

An EXPIRE parameter limits how long the URL is valid, preventing indefinite reuse. The IMAP server should accept URLs with an expiration of one hour or less without rejecting them. The RFC warns that anonymous URLs passed through SIP or MSCML can be intercepted by proxies, and recommends using SIPS (TLS-secured SIP) to protect the URL in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket is like a key that expires after an hour. You can give it to someone you trust (stream mode) or to anyone (anonymous), but if it goes through untrusted paths, use encryption to protect it.

sections.title: Transcoding and Media Compatibility
sections.content:
The client and media server negotiate supported media codecs using SDP (the Session Description Protocol) in the SIP exchange. The media server may need to transcode (convert) the media to a codec supported by the client. For example, if the IMAP server stores a video in one format and the client's device only supports another, the media server performs the conversion.

If the client and media server cannot find a common codec, or if the media server cannot transcode to a suitable format, the streaming attempt fails with an error. This negotiation process ensures that devices with different capabilities can still stream attachments.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for a video in format A but only speak format B, the helper translates it for you on the fly.
